title: SGS 2026: Newsrooms collaboration, data safeguards a must in new AI age
summary: ‘We need to become stronger newsrooms working together,’ SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe says

MacArthur Foundation Journalism and Media Director Kathy Im, and Rappler Executive Editor Glenda Gloria discuss the challenges and crossroads that newsrooms must face amid the rise of AI platforms during the We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

‘We need to become stronger newsrooms working together,’ SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe says

items: Philippine newsrooms face challenges such as declining trust in traditional media, a shrinking workforce, and the impact of AI on news consumption, prompting calls for stronger collaboration and regulation.
Despite the rise of AI, journalism remains essential for providing context and empathy in reporting, as AI cannot replace the human touch needed in storytelling during crises.
There is a push for legal protections for journalistic content against AI exploitation, and a need for global funding to support independent journalism, particularly in the global south.

CEBU, Philippines – Amid the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) around the globe, stronger collaborations among newsrooms and safety nets on the use of new technologies must be prioritized, SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe said during the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21.

Galarpe explained that Philippine newsrooms navigate a mix of challenges—ranging from a shrinking workforce to a decline in news website traffic—which are only worsened by a lack of regulation on social media platforms, hazardous working conditions due to disasters and AI data scrapers.

According to the Reuters Digital News Report 2026, the Philippines reported a 10% drop in trust in traditional media sources from the past year, marking the largest dip among countries included in the study.
“The lives of reporters are at stake in getting stories but trust in them is declining. That those who are scraping content are getting more trust is off-tangent,” the editor-in-chief added.

But this drop in media trust and website traffic isn’t just a phenomenon experienced solely by the Philippines, Wahyu Dyhatmika, chief executive officer of Tempo Digital and co-founder of IndonesiaLeaks.id, shared.

“After the AI overview lounge at the end of 2024, I think there is a zero-click phenomenon. People’s behavior in consuming news is also changing and people just don’t click through anymore,” Dyhatmika said.
The “AI disruption,” according to the Tempo Digital CEO, has pushed some Indonesian newsrooms to implement the use of digital guardrails that prevent the misuse of data by AI platforms.

“We need to protect our most important assets, our stories, our news articles, our archives and these cannot fall into the hands of other entities that can exploit it commercially without our consent and proper licensing,” Dyhatmika added.
Despite the challenges, Galarpe emphasized that journalism remains a valued force in the community, especially during calamities.

“When disaster happens, we need reporters who can show empathy to the victims and report the pain of vulnerable communities. AI cannot do this and if we rely on AI, it will just keep on saying yes, [and give] affirmation of what you want to hear,” Galarpe said.

The Cebu-based editor noted that even while a lack of regulation in social media platforms allows users to “compete” with journalists in breaking the news, it’s still journalists who are able to explain the context and causes of issues that matter to readers.
Unlike summaries provided by AI, Dyhatmika said journalists provide the credibility and integrity needed for information to be trusted by news consumers.

“We need to be a trusted voice in this [information] ecosystem and I think once we identify that, once we agree, that that is our strongest value, let’s build our business model around it,” Dyhatmika added.
Now more than ever, Galarpe said, newsrooms must collaborate with each other to combat the rise of AI-assisted disinformation networks.
“I want to stress that collaboration should strengthen, not dilute our independence. We do not need to become one newsroom. We need to become stronger newsrooms working together,” Galarpe said.
The SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief shared that a cooperation framework among regional newsrooms in the Philippines is in the works.
For Indonesia, Dyhatmika said that publishers there are now lobbying for revisions to the country’s copyright laws that would protect journalistic content from the exploitation of AI platforms.
Kathy Im, director of journalism and media at the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, shared during the summit that the work of foundations must reach newsrooms in the global south.

“In the American context, we have philanthropy and in the European context, there is a long tradition of private foundations and donors supporting journalism and that’s one thing I don’t see across the global south,” Im said.

Over the years, Im shared that funding for journalism has gone toward the protection of journalists, adding that this has become more prevalent as journalists in the United States are beginning to experience the plight of journalists in the global south due to a rise in authoritarian leadership and inhospitable environments.

“Information does not care about borders and those who spread mis- and disinformation don’t care about and don’t honor borders so our funding of journalism should be free of the borders of the US, and we should begin to fund globally to support independent journalism all over the world,” Im said. – Rappler.com
